faq: Do I need a product manager to use this?
No. Many founders and small teams use it for exactly that reason. We ask the questions a product manager would and keep the output simple enough for a team of two to follow.
Can you plan around a fixed deadline?
Yes. Tell us the date and what must be ready, and we work backwards, showing what fits and what slips. If the deadline is unrealistic, we say so early.
Which tools do you put the backlog in?
Jira, Trello, Linear, Notion, GitHub Projects or a plain spreadsheet. Tell us what you use. We never need your password, only an invite to the project.
Will you build what is on the roadmap?
If you want, yes. The other services on this page cover building and releasing features. The roadmap is yours either way, and you can give it to any developer or agency.
desc:
A product without a plan gets built by whoever shouted last. Ecom Swift LLC provides product roadmap planning for SaaS: a quarterly roadmap tied to your business goals, with effort estimates, ranked priorities and the trade-offs written down.

## What is a product roadmap for a SaaS business?

A product roadmap is a short document that shows what you intend to build, in what order and why. It links each feature or fix to a business goal, such as keeping customers, winning a segment or reducing support work.

A good roadmap is not a promise of dates. It is a ranked statement of intent that the team can discuss, challenge and update as facts change.

## Why planning matters before building

Development time is the scarcest thing most SaaS teams have. If it goes to whatever is loudest, you end up with a product shaped by the last conversation. Features are half finished, requests from one customer crowd out the needs of many and nobody can explain why one item was chosen over another.

Planning also protects relationships. When a customer asks for a feature, a roadmap gives you a straight answer: it is planned, it is later or it does not fit, and here is the reason. That is easier on everyone than a vague maybe.

## How a roadmap improves decisions and delivery

The benefit is focus. When every item has a goal, an estimate and an owner, the team can see what fits the available time and what does not. Dependencies surface early, so a task that blocks three others gets scheduled first. Risky items are flagged before they eat a sprint.

It improves communication too. Founders, developers, support and sales can read the same page. Disagreements move from opinions to trade-offs: if we add this, what leaves? That question is hard to ask without a visible plan.

## What a useful roadmap includes

- The business goals for the quarter, in plain words.
- A list of candidate features, fixes and technical work, collected from every source.
- A rough effort estimate for each item.
- A ranking by value, risk and effort, with the reasoning shown.
- Dependencies between items.
- An owner for each item.
- A clear line between what fits your team's time and what does not.
- Success measures for each theme, in the larger packages.
- A short note on trade-offs, so saying no has a reason attached.
- A backlog in the tool your team already uses.

## How we work

We begin with a goals session, where we ask what the business needs this quarter and what has not worked so far. We then gather your candidate items from tickets, notes and your own list. We estimate them, rank them and test the ranking with you.

The Basic package gives you a goals session, a ranked list and a one-page roadmap with a note on trade-offs. Standard adds a longer session, estimates for more items, mapped dependencies, owners and a backlog sheet in your tool. Premium adds two sessions, more items, best, likely and tight scenarios, success measures per theme, a summary for leadership and a backlog loaded into your tracker.

Building the roadmap items is a separate service. You can take the plan to any developer, including your own team.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Bring real goals, not only feature ideas.
- Share your support tickets and customer requests.
- Be open about team size and available hours.
- Name the deadlines that are truly fixed.
- Revisit the roadmap when the quarter ends.

**Avoid:**
- Filling every week of the quarter, which leaves no room for surprises.
- Treating the roadmap as a contract with customers.
- Ranking by who asked loudest.
- Mixing vague wishes and concrete tasks in one list.
- Planning far ahead in detail when little is known.

## Who this is for

This suits a founder who also acts as product manager and has no time to plan. It suits a small team that argues about priorities every week. It also suits a company preparing to brief investors or a new development partner on what comes next.

## What we need from you

Time for the planning session, your current list of ideas and any customer requests, and a note on how many developer hours you have. Access to your tracker as a team user helps if you want the backlog loaded there. We never need passwords.
